title: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum
word: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum
hook: gray light over the temple roof, one last worship, and food handed to someone else before the fast is broken
carry: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum

segments.voice: Yesterday in Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum: the offering, water, bilva, a wild flower, small so the care can be large. What small thing did you give away? Today the night ends, and so does this part of the path. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-nine.

The sky over the temple roof goes from black to slate to a thin, washed gray. Birds start before anyone else does. In the courtyard, people who have been up all night stand, stretch, wince, and gather for one last round of worship. The bell rings. The lamp is waved. Then a woman near the gate unties a cloth bundle she's been carrying since yesterday. There's food inside, and she has been fasting for a full day. She doesn't eat it. She hands it out first, to the people beside her, to the man sweeping the steps. Only then does she take a bite herself. Today, the last lesson of the night curriculum: what you do when the night is over.
screen: `BLACK, SLATE, GRAY.` → `ONE LAST WORSHIP.` → `FOOD HANDED OUT FIRST.`

segments.voice: Breaking a fast at the right time has a name: parana. In the Shiva Purana's account of the vow, the night doesn't end with the last song. The next morning there's worship again, and giving, and only then is the fast broken. So the vow closes the way it opened, on purpose. That ending matters. A night like this can turn into a story you tell about yourself: I stayed up, I didn't eat. The morning undoes that. It sends you straight back to ordinary things, food, a tired body, other people's hunger, and asks you to bring the night with you. If the night was about attention, the morning is where it's tested. Here's the whole course, start to finish. A resolve made in daylight. A fast that turns hunger into a bell. A vigil kept together. A name repeated through the dark. Offerings small enough to give completely. And a morning that hands the night back to ordinary life. And that closes more than the night. It closes this part of the path, the part about Shiva. We read selections of the Shiva Purana: the pillar no one could measure, Sati who would not hear him mocked, Parvati's tapas. We stood in front of Nataraja, the dancer. We walked through names from the Shiva Sahasranama. We opened Kashmir Shaivism through the Shiva Sutras. We lived inside the Rudram, bowing until the kind name appeared. And we kept one great night. Tomorrow the path turns from a god to a way of thinking: the six darshanas, schools of Hindu thought, set side by side and never ranked. First, Nyaya, the school of logic.
screen: `PARANA: BREAKING THE FAST.` · `WORSHIP, GIVING, THEN FOOD.` · `THE MORNING TESTS THE NIGHT.` · `THE SHIVA PART, GATHERED UP.` · then, large: `BRING THE NIGHT WITH YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a dawn sit. Settle, and breathe, as if the night has just ended and the light is coming up. Walk back through the night's lessons slowly: the resolve, the fast, the vigil, the name, the offering. Notice which one stayed with you. Hold that one. Then think of the first ordinary thing you'll do after this sit, a meal, a message, a walk to the door, and decide to carry that one lesson into it. If you pray, you can give thanks to Shiva, or to the God you know, for the night. The bell holds the time.
Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum. The last lesson: parana, the morning, when worship and giving come first, the fast is broken, and the night goes back out into ordinary life.
Your line: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum. Today, before your first meal or your first coffee, give something to someone else first, even a little. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: The morning after Maha Shivaratri, those who kept the fast worship again, may give food or gifts, and then break the fast with a simple meal; temples may distribute prasad to the people who kept the night.
